questions.question: What does a HashSet use internally to store its elements?
options: An array that it sorts after each add
A private HashMap, with each element stored as a key
A doubly linked list of nodes
questions.explanation: HashSet wraps a HashMap. Each element is a key and every key maps to one shared dummy value named PRESENT.

questions.question: What does this print? Set<String> s = new HashSet<>(); s.add("Zinc"); System.out.println(s.add("Zinc") + " " + s.size());
questions.explanation: The second add finds an equal element already stored, so it returns false and the size stays at 1.

questions.question: Which two methods does HashSet use to decide that two elements are duplicates?
questions.explanation: hashCode() picks the bucket and equals() checks the elements in it. TreeSet, not HashSet, uses compareTo.

questions.question: A Dose class overrides equals() but not hashCode(). Two equal Dose objects are added to a HashSet. What goes wrong?
options: The set sorts them and keeps one
Both are usually stored, because their default hash codes differ
questions.explanation: Object's hashCode gives each instance its own code, so equal objects go to different buckets and equals() is never compared.

questions.question: What does this print? Set<Integer> s = new HashSet<>(); s.add(null); s.add(null); s.add(5); System.out.println(s.size());
questions.explanation: HashSet allows a single null element. The second null is a duplicate, so the set holds null and 5.

questions.question: What is the average time cost of contains() on a HashSet with n elements?
questions.explanation: The element's hash code leads straight to one bucket, so only a few elements are compared on average.

questions.question: A Parcel object is added to a HashSet, then its weight field, which is part of hashCode(), is changed. Why does set.contains(parcel) now return false?
options: HashSet copies elements when they are added
The new hash code points to a different bucket than the one where it was stored
contains only works for String elements
Changing a field removes the element automatically
questions.explanation: The element still sits in the bucket chosen by its old hash code. The lookup uses the new code and searches elsewhere.

questions.question: You need unique items printed in the same order you added them. Which class fits best?
questions.explanation: LinkedHashSet keeps a linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order while lookups stay O(1).

questions.question: What does this print? Set<String> a = new HashSet<>(Arrays.asList("Iron", "Zinc")); a.retainAll(Arrays.asList("Zinc", "Folic")); System.out.println(a);
questions.explanation: retainAll keeps only the elements that are also in the other collection, which is the intersection. Only Zinc is shared.

questions.question: Why does a HashSet have no get(int index) method?
options: It is too slow to implement
A set has no positions; elements sit in hash buckets, not at indexes
questions.explanation: Elements are placed by hash code, not by position, so an index would be meaningless. Loop over the set or copy it into a list.
